data.text/markdown:
Monte Carlo localization with a particle filter

This notebook uses the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3) to localize a simulated robot on the known map of an office, from its odometry and 2D laser scans. It uses these MRPT modules:
  • mrpt.maps: the map (COccupancyGridMap2D inside a CMultiMetricMap), configured with mrpt.config.CConfigFileMemory.
  • mrpt.obs: odometry (CActionRobotMovement2D, CActionCollection) and laser scans (CObservation2DRangeScan, CSensoryFrame).
  • mrpt.slam and mrpt.bayes: the particle filter (CMonteCarloLocalization2D, CParticleFilter).
Monte Carlo localization (MCL) represents the belief about the robot pose with thousands of particles, each one a pose hypothesis. Choose global localization (the robot could be anywhere) or tracking (the initial pose is roughly known), then move the time slider to watch the particles converge. The filter runs once per parameter set; the time slider only selects which step to draw.

data.text/html: Parameters

data.text/markdown:
1. The map

MCL needs a map. Here it is drawn from the floor plan: the cells crossed by walls are set as occupied, the rest of the building as free. The map lives in a CMultiMetricMap created from an INI-style configuration, the usual way to set MRPT map options. The likelihoodOpts section sets how scans are scored against the map (a likelihood field): using only one of every 20 rays and a wide σ gives a smoother likelihood, which makes global localization more robust.

2. Odometry and laser scans

At each step the robot moves 30 cm and reads its odometry, with an error of 2 cm and 1° (σ). CActionRobotMovement2D.computeFromOdometry() turns each odometry increment into a probabilistic motion model, here a Gaussian whose uncertainty must be at least as large as the real odometry error. Each laser scan goes into a CSensoryFrame, the set of observations taken at that step.

3. Running the particle filter

Each call to CParticleFilter.executeOn(pdf, action, frame) runs one step of MCL: every particle is moved by a random sample of the motion model (prediction), weighted by how well the scan fits the map from that pose (update), and the set is resampled so that unlikely particles die and likely ones multiply. With KLD sampling, the number of particles adapts to how spread out the belief is.

data.text/markdown:
Things to try
  • In global localization, the particles first survive in all the places that look alike (rooms with a similar shape, the corridor), and the mean is meaningless. They collapse into one cluster once the robot sees a distinctive part of the office.
  • With few particles (1000 to 3000), often no particle starts close enough to the true pose and the filter converges to a wrong place: change the random seed to see it. Tracking from a known pose works even with 300 particles.
  • With KLD sampling, the number of particles drops by an order of magnitude once the belief becomes concentrated, which makes each step much faster.

Run it on your computer (Linux, Python 3.11 to 3.14): 
uvx marimo edit --sandbox https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MRPT/mrpt-notebooks/main/notebooks/monte_carlo_localization.py
More MRPT Python examples: mrpt_examples_py.
